content:
In a \(2n\times 2n\) grid a cell‑loop is the set of cells that form the border of an \(a\times b\) rectangle, where \(a,b\ge 2\).  
A partition of the whole grid into several loops can be obtained only by successively taking the border of a rectangle that touches the current outer boundary of the still‑un‑filled part of the grid.  
Indeed, if a chosen rectangle does not touch the outer boundary, it would leave a strip of width \(1\) (or more) that can never be filled by a loop (every loop has width at least \(2\)).  
Consequently each loop must be the border of a rectangle that uses the whole current height or whole current width; the rectangle’s inner area is then a smaller rectangle that will be partitioned in the same way.

Starting with a \(10\times 10\) grid we are forced to choose the outermost loop as the whole boundary \(10\times 10\).  
Its inner unused rectangle has size \(8\times 8\).  
Repeating the argument for the \(8\times 8\) rectangle forces the next loop to be its whole boundary \(8\times 8\); the interior is a \(6\times 6\) rectangle.  
Again the next loop must be the whole \(6\times 6\) boundary, leaving a \(4\times 4\) rectangle; its loop is the whole \(4\times 4\) boundary, leaving a \(2\times 2\) rectangle; finally its loop is the whole \(2\times 2\) boundary.  

Thus the only possible way to partition a \(10\times 10\) grid into loops is the nested sequence

\[
10\times10\rightarrow8\times8\rightarrow6\times6\rightarrow4\times4\rightarrow2\times2 .
\]

No alternative choice of rectangles is possible, so there is exactly one partition.

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
